title: Counterexample Generation via Per-Theorem Symbolic Verifiers: When Imitation Hurts and Reinforcement Repairs
summary: Large language models often solve a theorem forward yet fail to disprove a closely related false one: a falsification gap that supervised fine-tuning does not close and can actively worsen. We frame counterexample generation as constrained witness emission against a deterministic per-theorem Python verifier, and release SymCE, a corpus of 4,707 false undergraduate-algebra and real-analysis conjectures, each paired with executable verifiers. The verifier also serves as the reward function, making SymCE a training environment. Training Qwen3-4B with SFT followed by GRPO under this oracle reveals an imitation trap: counterexample-only SFT collapses true-theorem recognition from 0.27 to 0.00, while RLVR with a sparse outcome-only reward repairs this and exceeds the base, to 0.66. The collapse replicates across four seeds and on Gemma-3-4B. Sparse and dense rewards yield statistically indistinguishable in-domain success yet diverge by 33 points on a held-out calibration probe, a dissociation we trace to the partial-credit term. Our 4B model outperforms every evaluated 7B open-weights math specialist, remains competitive with six frontier commercial APIs, and transfers under unchanged prompting to GSM8K, MATH-500 and MMLU-college-math. A human audit of 177 verifier decisions finds 97.7% accuracy. Code, data, verifier modules and annotations: https://github.com/ce-rlvr/SymCE.

title: Viva La Vida: Verification and Accumulation Failures in Multi-Agent Proof Search
summary: When an agentic prover works on an open problem, there is no proof assistant to fall back on: its verifier and lemma library are ultimately language models judging model outputs. We instrumented such a system end to end and analyzed $51{,}754$ traced observations across three full runs ($186$ hours, \$$5{,}694$). We find three connected failure modes. First, the three-model verifier requires unanimity and treats parse or API failure as non-approval; in $10$ of $12$ verification events, one member returned no parseable output or an API error, making acceptance arithmetically impossible without surfacing an error. Second, when the ensemble did function, one verifier approved $3$ attempts that GPT rejected, each claiming to resolve the open problem; a single-verifier design would therefore have announced a solution three times. Third, because nothing could be approved, every review was a refutation, yet the lemma extractor mines reviews as well as proofs: $24$ of $93$ lemmas ($26\%$) were extracted from rejected arguments with their refutational context removed. Taken together, these findings show that without external verification, supervision is itself a critical trust boundary: systems must distinguish abstention from rejection, preserve useful disagreement, and preserve the provenance and polarity of information before it becomes future context.

title: Optimal bound for the polynomial Littlewood-Offord problem
summary: We present an exposition of an argument, discovered by GPT-6 Pro, that gives an optimal bound for the polynomial Littlewood-Offord problem. Namely, let $F$ be a degree-$d$ multilinear polynomial that contains $r$ degree-$d$ monomials involving disjoint sets of variables. Then, for i.i.d. Rademacher random variables $ξ_1, \ldots, ξ_n$, we have $\mathbb{P}[F(ξ_1, \ldots, ξ_n) = 0] = O_d(r^{-1/2})$. This improves upon the previous bound of $(\log r)^{O_d(1)} r^{-1/2}$ due to Meka, O. Nguyen, and Vu, and resolves a conjecture attributed to H. Nguyen and Vu. The key part of the proof is an estimate for the total influence of bounded-degree rational functions, which resolves a recent conjecture of Kothari, Kovacs-Deak, Wang, and Yang.

title: Bolzano: From Expert-Guided Proof Search to Automated Open-Problem Solving
summary: Large language models are increasingly contributing to mathematical research, where progress often depends on efficient proof search, incremental improvements and careful verification. We describe Bolzano, a multi-agent open-source system that uses parallel prover agents with a verifier agent and maintains a human-readable research state. Initial manual use on expert-selected problems yielded 8 results whose proofs were checked by domain experts. Motivated by these case studies, we ran Bolzano without problem-specific human guidance on about 3,800 open problems extracted from four sets of papers, solving about 200 open problems. One experiment used papers accepted to STOC 2026, a top conference in theoretical computer science. There, we answered four questions raised in the papers, as confirmed by their authors.

title: Fault-tolerant foundation models
summary: Emerging computer hardware often trades reliability for energy efficiency; here we show that large-language models (LLMs) can be trained to tolerate this unreliability, and that rather than degrading, their error resilience actually increases as they grow. Modified neural scaling laws inferred from 40,000 GPU-hours of training runs on simulated faulty digital hardware quantify this trend and suggest that models learn to compute within "good" error-correcting codes, whose relative overhead remains finite no matter how large the model gets. This finding leads us to conjecture that appropriately trained LLMs may be formally fault-tolerant; if true, running AI inference on low energy, faulty hardware may be a path to substantial energy savings over the status quo.

title: A Society of Researchers: Designing Institutions for Populations of Autonomous Research Agents
summary: Deployments of research agents are moving to populations of thousands that share one pool of compute, while most current systems organize one project at a time or leave the population unorganized. We argue that such a population will acquire an organization whether or not its designers provide one, so designers should provide it explicitly, and that the multi-agent systems community holds the tools to do so. We propose a society of agents, a population of persistent agents under explicit institutions, and develop it for science as a society of researchers built on six principles. Principal investigators compete for compute through requests for proposals, independent review, and grants; a human governor, the mayor, allocates resources and assigns no tasks. In a running society of ten thousand researchers, asked only to improve the pretraining of language models, one lab reported a way to reach the same quality with about 30% less compute, a result the labs that tested it do not yet agree on. We close with six open problems for the agents community.

title: Agentic-TTT: Training test-time policy for test-time training
summary: Test-time training (TTT) adapts an LLM's parameters using signals derived from test inputs, and can make striking improvements in pre-specified settings such as IMO competitions or designated open problems. By turning deployment experience into parameter updates, TTT provides a direct mechanism for model-level self-improvement. Yet TTT is not universally beneficial: each TTT algorithm works in different settings, and applying an ill-suited method could waste test-time compute or even damage model performance. Therefore, such parameter-level self-improvement requires agency: the model must decide when TTT is warranted, which algorithm to invoke, and whether an existing skill can be reused. To fill this gap, we introduce Agentic-TTT, which learns a test-time policy to govern those decisions. Agentic-TTT turns TTT procedures into callable tools, treats accumulated skills as an evolving deployment environment, and trains its policy using the observed utility gains from its decisions. On our benchmark, Agentic-TTT nearly doubles the utility over the backbone model, learns to trade off utility against compute, and generalizes to domains unseen during training. Together, these results point toward autonomous self-improvement: models that can decide how to learn from their own deployment experience.

title: Unlocking the Regulatory Genome by ARGUS: An Evidence-Constrained Agentic Framework for Interpreting Single Nucleotide Variants
summary: Over 90% of disease-associated variants from genome-wide association studies fall in noncoding regulatory regions, yet their functional interpretation remains a central open problem in genomic medicine. Large language models prompted to interpret such variants routinely hallucinate transcription factor (TF) binding changes, fabricate experimental support, and assign biological significance to statistically negligible signals. ARGUS wraps 458 DNABERT-based TF binding models in a hypothesis-directed investigation loop where a planner selects evidence sources based on current uncertainty, a verifier deterministically interprets each observation, and intermediate results change the investigation path. title: SqueezeBench: Saturation-Resilient Evaluation of Mathematical Capability
summary: AI systems are making rapid progress in mathematics, but this progress is hard to measure. Benchmarks of solved problems saturate, and in benchmarks of open problems each problem can be resolved for the first time only once. We present SqueezeBench, a benchmark that is resilient to saturation: a success raises the bar instead of removing the problem. Each problem fixes an integer function $f(n)$ whose values are known only for small $n$, and the benchmark keeps a lower and an upper record on it. A record is a computable Lean function with a machine-checked proof that it bounds $f$. A submission proposes a new function and proves that it bounds $f$, that it is no worse than the current record at any $n$, and that it is strictly better at some $n$. Once accepted, it becomes the record that the next submission has to beat. The system thus chooses the bound as well as its proof, and it may improve the record at a single $n$ or its growth rate. At every $n$, the gap between the two records shows how far the certified bounds are from determining $f(n)$. Every proof is checked by two independent Lean kernels, so no referee needs to check the mathematics. The checks also reject a function that computes $f$ by exhaustive search at small $n$, and a maintainer only reads the submitter's report and looks for such a search at larger $n$. title: Quadratic-size Random Permutations are Universal
summary: A permutation is $n$-universal if it contains every permutation of length $n$ as a pattern. We prove that a uniformly random permutation of length $32n^2$ is $n$-universal with probability at least $1-\exp(-c n/\log n)$, for an absolute constant $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$. This removes a $\log\log n$ factor from an earlier result of He and Kwan~\cite{He-Kwan} and resolves an open problem of Alon~\cite{Alon2016}. The proof was found by GPT-6 Pro.

title: Humanize Olympiad Agents: A Multi-Session Workflow for Olympiad Problem Solving with Solve, Review, Wiki, Verify
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly improving on long-horizon scientific and olympiad tasks. Recent systems have produced a Lean-formalized resolution of the Navier--Stokes problem and autonomous solutions to four open questions in the Erdős Conjectures database. Yet neither system releases both its underlying model and complete inference stack. More broadly, a single agent session remains brittle on difficult problems: early errors can propagate, missing domain knowledge can stall progress, and apparent success can mask a misinterpretation or weakening of the original task. We introduce HOA (Humanize Olympiads Agent), an open, flow-level framework that coordinates multiple agent sessions through three complementary feedback channels. First, an independent reviewer evaluates each candidate and provides actionable feedback. Second, a structured wiki supplies task-specific knowledge that may be missing or unreliable in model pretraining. Third, a verifier checks generated Lean proofs against trusted challenge statements. With GPT-5.6 Sol, HOA achieves perfect scores on the IMO, IPhO, and IOI 2026, near-full marks on the IChO 2026 problem set, and solves all 672 problems (100%) on PutnamBench. On the Lean-Eval leaderboard, HOA ranks first, solving 251 of 304 problems (82.6%). We further evaluate HOA with open models. title: Deep learning from a control vantage point
summary: This article offers an overview of recent developments in deep learning from a control vantage point. It reviews several classes of models including feedforward and residual neural networks, transformers, large-language models, and selective state space models while explaining how control theory plays an important role in understanding their training, properties, or architecture design. The article explains how residual neural networks can be interpreted as the discretization of a continuous-time control system thereby enabling the use of control theoretic techniques for its analysis. To illustrate the power of this bridge between control and deep learning, two technical results are discussed: 1) the ability of a residual neural network to approximate arbitrary continuous functions is a non-standard controllability problem that can be solved using geometric nonlinear control and 2) transformers, the key architectural component of most large language-models, can be seen the discretization of a consensus algorithm and thus large language-models exhibit consensus. Another point of contact between control theory and deep learning is the connection between backpropagation, the algorithm used to train neural networks, and optimal control. title: Where Polanyi Meets Galois: Tacit Knowing as an Algebro-Deterministic Operation, Toward Re-rooting AI-Generated Science
summary: We argue that tacit knowing is better modelled as an operating regime of a memory than as a kind of content. Our substrate is VaCoAl, an algebro-deterministic XOR-and-shift hyperdimensional memory over GF(2), realized as CASRAM and PyVaCoAl. In it, a DAG reads two ways. Repairing every collision (Rescue) makes the trace exactly auditable but ranks no path higher; tolerating them (Don't Care) yields a path confidence, CR$_2$, silently favouring direct routes. This audit-valuation complementarity formalizes Polanyi's claim that tacit and explicit are not sharply divided. It separates contingent tacitness, which a new query brings out (AlphaGo's game tree), from regime-bound tacitness, statable only once it is gone (AlphaGo's hunches). (1) Polanyi's from-to structure reads as non-commutative binding. (2) Explicating the valuation destroys it, as with Polanyi's pianist, yet a closed-form law states it. Polanyi, Nonaka, Tsoukas and Collins each capture part of this, narrowly; even Nonaka and von Krogh's continuum cannot tell the classes apart. (3) Collins's three tacit knowledges become strata, one outside the substrate. (4) Our mentor-student DAG is a tacit-transmission graph. title: A Lean formalisation of the disproof of Ramaekers's conjecture
summary: We describe Redhill, a Lean formalisation of the major results in Hölzl, Kleine and Stephan's "Improved Lower Bounds for Strong $n$-Conjectures" (arXiv:2409.13439). Design decisions regarding types and data structures are justified as enabling canonical versions of the paper's claims, and from there the most direct proofs of said claims. The formalisation process also uncovered many errors, omissions and optimisation opportunities in the informal proof, all of which are addressed in the final library. Although Redhill is meant to stand alone, a few lemmas were upstreamed to the primary Lean mathematics library mathlib. We discuss the tension between upstreaming and leaving lemmas in separate libraries. Unlike many other contemporary formalisation projects, Redhill was completed without any assistance from large language models (LLMs). We compare our work with LLM-assisted projects, in particular an extension of arXiv:2409.13439 to $n=4$, aiming to establish design and style guidelines that define good Lean formalisations.

title: On the Monitorability of Natural Language Autoencoders: Identification vs Discrimination

We formalise NLA training and NLA oversight deployment as two different referential games from Emergent Communication: training is a generative referential game, while oversight is a discriminative, multi-modal, partially-observable referential game played over a many-to-many relation between the monitored language model's activations and the accounts that are true of them. title: Szemerédi's theorem with random differences and arithmetic Kakeya
summary: We prove that there exists an absolute constant $c > 0$ such that the following holds for every $k \ge 3$ and $p \ge n^{-c / \log \log k}$. Letting $δ> 0$ and $D \sim [n]_p$, with high probability every ${S \subset [n]}$ with $|S| \ge δn$ contains a $k$-term arithmetic progression whose common difference lies in $D$. This improves the best known bounds for the threshold of Szemerédi's theorem with random differences for all sufficiently large $k$, previously of the form ${p \ge n^{-2/k+o(1)}}$, due to Briët and Castro-Silva. We obtain our improvement via a small cover lemma, in the sense of Alon and Pham's work on random Cayley graphs, and its proof crucially relies on a construction of Green and Ruzsa in the context of the arithmetic Kakeya conjecture. The usage of the latter was suggested to us by GPT 6 Astra.

title: Typed Decision Models on Tabular Data
summary: Typed decision models are language models that answer a question with a fixed set of possible answers by returning a probability for each answer instead of generating text. We study them on tabular data and compare four decision models with three large language models (LLMs) on row classification, fact verification and anomaly detection. Every request is sent in its original form and under 21 types of rewrite that keep its content, such as renaming the options or writing the table in another format. The decision models perform as well as the LLMs at a lower cost. Three of them are also far more robust to how the question is formulated. No model we test is robust to how the table is organized. For every model, at least a third of the row decisions change under some rewrite of the table or the question. The decisions to which a decision model gives low probability are the ones most likely to change. Decision models are a practical choice for tabular decisions, but their robustness remains an open problem.

title: IneqAgent: Agentic Inequality Proving in Lean with Symbolic Computation
summary: Formal inequality proving requires mathematical reasoning and exact computation, often connected through intermediate lemmas and goal reformulations. We introduce IneqAgent, an agentic framework combining LLM reasoning with symbolic computation for inequality proving in Lean4. Lemma-level Monte Carlo Tree Search coordinates lemma construction, goal reformulation, and symbolic backend selection. Complementary sum-of-squares, Bernstein, and successive difference-substitution backends produce exact certificates for local Lean proof generation. The agent integrates these proofs with LLM-generated steps and uses Lean feedback to construct complete proofs checked against the original theorem statements. On four benchmarks, IneqAgent with DeepSeek-V4-Flash solves 175 of 186 problems (94.09%), achieving the highest overall success rate among the evaluated methods. Across four backbones, it achieves higher success rates at low LLM inference cost thresholds than Direct Agent using the same backbone, with lower mean inference costs over each method's successful runs. We also obtain Lean-verified strengthenings of Dittert's conjecture in dimensions four and five, and certify the Holens--Djokovic $(4,4)$ inequality, implying Merris's conjecture in dimension four.

To push beyond static challenges, we explore the Busy Beaver (BB) domain, an uncomputable frontier that is fundamentally open-ended. title: The maximum number of Hamiltonian cycles in tournaments
summary: Let $C(n)$ denote the maximum number of directed Hamiltonian cycles in a tournament on $n$ vertices. We prove that, as $n\to\infty$, $$ C(n) = \left(\frac{\cosh 1}{\cos 1}\pm o(1)\right)\frac{(n-1)!}{2^n}. $$ The bound is asymptotically attained by the regular tournament with vertices $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ where $(i,j)$ is a directed edge if $j - i \pmod n< n/2$. This answers a question of Alon and proves a conjecture of Wormald. Among the other implications of these results is asymptotically determining the maximum number of Hamiltonian paths in a tournament on $n$ vertices. We provide our own exposition of these proofs, which were originally found by GPT-5.6.

title: Claims of emergence in AI should be grounded in information decomposition
summary: When a language model develops capabilities not traceable to its individual components, when a multi-agent AI system outperforms each agent on its own, or when a human-AI pair succeeds where either fails in isolation, AI researchers describe it as a case of ``synergy'' or ``emergence''. However, these are usually informal assessments not supported by a theoretical framework, making these claims impossible to compare or even meaningfully dispute. Here we argue that \emph{information decomposition can serve as a unifying formal framework to operationalize assessments about synergy in AI systems}. Information decomposition provides a way to distinguish qualitatively different \emph{types} of information, including unique information available from individual components, redundant information shared across multiple components, and synergistic information accessible only from parts taken together. This gives claims of emergence a precise, falsifiable criterion: a system's behavior is emergent only if it carries synergistic information about task-relevant outcomes. We apply this lens to attention heads, autonomous agents, and human-AI teams, showing how it organizes existing knowledge across scales and substrates, while also generating cross-level conjectures that siloed fields would miss.

title: ARCANA: A Benchmark for Abstraction and Analogical Reasoning
summary: Analogical reasoning is widely considered a fundamental component of human intelligence. Few benchmarks are designed to explicitly test far analogical reasoning - reasoning between domains that are superficially dissimilar yet share deep relational or structural similarities. In this work, we introduce an analogical reasoning benchmark called Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus of ANAlogy (ARCANA). The tasks of ARCANA require performing far analogical mappings from real-world objects or physical phenomena to abstract grid-based transformations, different from the well-known ARC-AGI benchmark which primarily emphasized innate human priors. We validate ARCANA through a human study, demonstrating that humans solve these tasks reliably. In contrast, evaluations across a range of large language models show a distinct performance gap compared to humans, revealing systematic failure modes that remain challenging for current models. To address this gap, we propose ConceptSIR, a reasoning framework based on concept slippage, introspection, and reflection. Experiments demonstrate that ConceptSIR enables standard LLMs to solve several challenging ARCANA tasks that were unsolved by direct prompting in our evaluation. Overall, our results suggest that far analogical reasoning remains an open problem for contemporary LLMs. All the materials are available at sites.google.com/view/arcanacogtest. The complete codebase, including benchmark, and ConceptSIR, is publicly available at https://github.

title: Detection Is Not Enough: Reasoning Traces as Testable Program Hypotheses
summary: When a language model is deployed, no reference solution exists, so the reasoning trace it writes is the only evidence for judging its answer. The reference-free substitutes each fail differently: self-assessment degrades the answer it was meant to protect, sampling agreement measures stability rather than correctness, and perturbation studies read the expected answer off a human-written template, grading a model rather than a trace. We ask how far a single trace can be verified with no reference solution, no judge model and no weight update, and find, for a frozen LLaMA-2-7B-chat on GSM8K, that detection is not what limits such a pipeline. Checking a trace against itself reaches an AUROC of 0.741 and stops there for a structural reason: two thirds of wrong traces state no false equation, having executed a mistaken plan correctly, and on wrong-plan failures the detector flags a wrong trace less often than a right one. A candidate-derived metamorphic probe exposes many of these failures: we abstract the trace into a program over the question's quantities, perturb one quantity, execute the program, and ask the model the rewritten question once, so every trace supplies its own test. Valid perturbations exist for 937 of 1,319 test questions (71.0%); among the 847 that also have a parseable first trace, supported traces are correct 60.6% of the time against a 31.6% base rate, although the probe also refutes 45.5% of correct traces.
